name: Tobii Pro Spectrum
tagline: High-speed tracking for the laboratory
description: A screen-based system for vision, cognition, and oculomotor research, with gaze sampling at up to 1200 Hz.
use: Microsaccades, reading, and gaze-contingent experiments
review: Temporal resolution is its main draw. Assess the complete setup, including synchronization hardware, experimental software, and tracking quality in your participant population.
specNote: Up to 1200 Hz; available modes depend on the configuration.

name: EyeLink 3
tagline: Integrated eye and head tracking for research
description: SR Research’s newer screen-based research system combines eye and head tracking at up to 1000 Hz, according to the manufacturer.
use: Head–eye coordination, reading, and cognitive science
review: The integrated design is worth evaluating. When migrating existing EyeLink experiments, check software versions, data fields, and end-to-end latency.
specNote: Up to 1000 Hz, depending on the operating mode.

name: Neon
tagline: Modular glasses powered by deep learning
description: Neon combines an eye-tracking module with interchangeable frames and provides gaze, pupil, and other eye-state signals.
use: Natural behavior, children, sports, and interaction prototypes
review: Calibration-free operation can reduce preparation time, but task-specific validation remains necessary. Evaluate cloud analysis, offline workflows, and data governance together.
specNote: NeonNet documentation lists gaze and eye-state data at 200 Hz; scene video is 30 Hz.

name: Tobii Pro Fusion
tagline: Portable screen-based research
description: A screen-based eye tracker designed for deployment across research locations, with sampling at up to 250 Hz.
use: UX, reading, behavioral experiments, and field deployments
review: A useful option when deployment flexibility matters. Before choosing it, check licensed sampling modes, SDK access, and analysis-software costs.
specNote: Up to 250 Hz; confirm the available modes and licenses.

name: EyeLink 1000 Plus
tagline: A configurable high-speed experiment platform
description: Uses a dedicated Host PC and offers multiple mounts and lenses, with integration options for neurophysiological equipment.
use: Microsaccades and combined EEG, fMRI, or MEG experiments
review: Its strengths are experimental control and configuration flexibility. Specify head-stabilized or head-free tracking, lenses, mounts, and synchronization requirements in the purchase configuration.
specNote: Up to 2000 Hz binocularly with the head stabilized; Remote tracking typically supports up to 1000 Hz.

name: Tobii Pro Glasses 3
tagline: Mobile recording in real-world settings
description: A glasses-based system that combines first-person scene video with eye-tracking data for observing behavior beyond a monitor.
use: Consumer behavior, sports, human factors, and field research
review: Natural activities are the main use case. Trial dynamic area-of-interest annotation, prescription-lens options, and the video-analysis workflow before committing.
specNote: Confirm the 50 / 100 Hz modes against the specific version.

name: Tobii Pro Spark
tagline: An entry point to screen-based research
description: Records gaze at 60 Hz and is positioned as an accessible system for attention and behavioral research.
use: Teaching, website UX, and attention analysis with large areas of interest
review: Useful for fixation distributions and dwell analysis. For fast saccade dynamics, first validate whether its temporal resolution meets the task requirements.
specNote: 60 Hz; sampling rate does not indicate spatial accuracy.

name: Tobii Glasses X
tagline: Eye-tracking glasses for training and activity
description: A wearable in Tobii’s current product catalog, positioned for attention recording in UX, sports, and industrial environments.
use: Skill training, sports, and industrial tasks
review: Evaluate field deployment and visualization workflows first. Do not assume its raw-data interfaces are identical to those of Pro Glasses 3.
specNote: No sampling-rate value is entered here without verification.

name: EyeLink Portable Duo
tagline: High-speed EyeLink recording beyond the lab
description: A portable screen-based system with head-stabilized and head-free modes that uses the EyeLink experimental-software ecosystem.
use: Off-site experiments, schools, and data collection across locations
review: Especially relevant for teams with existing EyeLink programs. Portable does not mean recording while walking: a display and suitable participant positioning are still required.
specNote: Up to 2000 Hz binocularly with the head stabilized; up to 1000 Hz with the head free to move.

name: Pupil Core
tagline: A wearable platform with open-source software
description: Modular head-mounted hardware works with open-source software, a network API, and Python plugins for programmable recording.
use: Research prototypes, method development, and custom integrations
review: Suited to developers who want control over acquisition. Allow time for calibration, camera adjustment, and maintaining your own analysis workflow.
specNote: Eye-camera rates and gaze-output rates differ; verify the hardware version.

name: Pupil Invisible
tagline: The calibration-free platform preceding Neon
description: Pupil Labs’ deep-learning eye-tracking glasses are now documented as a legacy platform replaced by Neon.
use: Reproducing existing datasets and comparing historical methods
review: Relevant when interpreting older studies. For used equipment, verify the companion phone, applications, cloud services, and maintenance status.
specNote: Legacy product; Neon specifications must not be applied to it.

name: Gazepoint GP3
tagline: Desktop tracking for teaching and basic analysis
description: Gazepoint’s screen-based eye tracker comes with an associated analysis-software ecosystem and developer interfaces.
use: Teaching demonstrations, website testing, and basic attention studies
review: Run a pilot with your own display, participants, and area-of-interest sizes. Include the analysis-software edition and licensing in the budget.
specNote: Distinguish GP3 from GP3 HD and confirm the exact model.

name: Smart Eye Pro
tagline: Multicamera tracking across larger spaces
description: A remote head- and eye-tracking system configurable with 2–8 cameras for more complex environments.
use: Driving, aviation, multiple displays, and control rooms
review: Worth evaluating for larger movement spaces and multiple display surfaces. Camera placement, calibration, and spatial mapping add engineering work compared with a single screen bar.
specNote: Depends on the cameras and system configuration; software version numbers are not sampling rates.

name: Smart Eye AI-X
tagline: Compact screen-based behavioral research
description: Smart Eye positions AI-X for screen-based studies in marketing, UX, and media.
use: Advertising, websites, and attention to media
review: Compare deployment workflows and the analysis ecosystem. Verify the raw outputs, synchronization options, and licenses required by your study.
specNote: Confirm sampling rate and supported display size in the current configuration sheet.

name: Smart Eye Aurora
tagline: Smart Eye’s remote bar-tracker platform
description: Aurora is a compact remote tracker in Smart Eye’s product portfolio for screen-related research.
use: Screen-based studies and existing Smart Eye projects
review: Official product information remains available, but configurations may differ by generation. Ask about current availability, firmware, and support.
specNote: Historical specifications are not treated as a single current configuration.

name: Dikablis Glasses X
tagline: Glasses for movement and challenging lighting
description: Dikablis Glasses X works with the Prophea.X workflow and emphasizes field, sports, and multimodal recording.
use: Driving, sports, occupational tasks, and human factors
review: Trial fit and synchronization with other sensors. The website’s eye- and scene-camera rate descriptions need to be checked separately against the data sheet.
specNote: The website contains both 60 Hz and “up to 120 Hz” descriptions; no single verified gaze-sampling rate is assigned here.

name: TRACKPixx3
tagline: Binocular tracking for vision experiments
description: A system comprising a high-speed camera, infrared illumination, mounting hardware, and a VPixx control unit, configurable in LabMaestro.
use: Visual psychophysics, gaze feedback, and synchronized experiments
review: Particularly relevant to labs with VPixx hardware. Budget for the control unit, lens, mounting hardware, and display as well as the tracker.
specNote: Consult the data sheet for sampling rate and short- or long-range lens configurations.

name: LiveTrack Lightning
tagline: Binocular recording for vision science
description: LiveTrack Lightning provides 500 Hz video-based eye tracking and can be combined with CRS stimulus-presentation equipment.
use: Saccades, pupillometry, and visual psychophysics
review: Evaluate the complete stimulus-presentation and recording chain. Validate head-position requirements, real-time interfaces, and synchronization.
specNote: Official documentation lists binocular recording at 500 Hz.

name: ViewPoint EyeTracker
tagline: The configurable ViewPoint platform
description: Arrington Research offers head-fixed, head-mounted, and custom-integration options; some configurations include ocular torsion measurements.
use: Vision experiments, torsion measurements, and custom integrations
review: The range of configurations offers flexibility, but price and performance depend on the specific system. Check older web specifications against the newer catalog item by item.
specNote: Up to 400 Hz applies to certain head-fixed configurations, not the entire product range.

name: Varjo XR-4 series
tagline: Integrated eye tracking for professional XR
description: The XR-4 series uses eye tracking for dynamic foveated rendering in professional simulation and mixed-reality environments.
use: Flight simulation, design reviews, and XR research
review: Consider it when professional imaging and simulation integration matter. Evaluate the workstation, software licenses, and eye-tracking outputs available through the SDK.
specNote: The manufacturer reports 200 Hz eye tracking; this is separate from display refresh rate.

name: VIVE Focus Vision
tagline: Integrated tracking for standalone and PC VR
description: VIVE Focus Vision integrates eye tracking and automatic IPD adjustment for compatible VR applications.
use: VR interaction, avatars, and foveated rendering
review: Confirm that the target application and operating mode expose the eye-tracking fields you need. Recalibration is required after changing IPD or headset position.
specNote: Display refresh rate is not used as a proxy for eye-tracking sampling rate.

name: VIVE Pro Eye
tagline: An established headset in VR research
description: VIVE Pro Eye integrates eye tracking and has been used in VR interaction and gaze-related research.
use: Reproducing existing VR experiments and SDK-based research
review: Confirm stock and support status, then check whether SRanipal, OpenXR, or the application-level interface works in your target environment.
specNote: Older platform; availability and software support require confirmation.

name: FOVE 0
tagline: An eye-tracking VR platform for developers
description: FOVE 0 provides eye-tracking data and SDKs for multiple languages, with Unity and Unreal integration options.
use: VR method development, gaze interaction, and analysis
review: Data interfaces are a main attraction. Display, positional tracking, and connection requirements also constrain experiment design, so trial the complete system.
specNote: Eye cameras: 120 Hz. Display: 70 Hz. These are different rates.

name: Pimax Crystal (original)
tagline: Tobii eye tracking in the original Crystal
description: The original Pimax Crystal supports automatic IPD and dynamic foveated rendering; official material lists 120 Hz eye tracking.
use: PC VR, simulation, and foveated rendering
review: Model identification is essential. This entry covers the original Crystal only and does not merge features from other Crystal products.
specNote: 120 Hz, according to documentation for the original model.

name: Apple Vision Pro
tagline: Spatial computing with eye and hand input
description: Vision Pro uses infrared cameras and LEDs for eye interaction, with gaze serving as a core system input.
use: Spatial interaction, interface design, and user experience
review: System-level interaction does not establish access to research data. Ordinary apps do not receive continuous gaze data directly; check eligibility and restrictions for specialized interfaces.
specNote: No eye-tracking sampling rate is inferred from display refresh rate.

name: HoloLens 2
tagline: An eye-tracking platform for optical-see-through AR
description: HoloLens 2 provides a standard gaze ray and extended eye-tracking interfaces, with user permission and calibration required.
use: AR interaction, industrial tasks, and reproducing existing studies
review: The API mode determines the available data. Distinguish the standard approximately 30 Hz output from extended 30 / 60 / 90 Hz modes, and check the device lifecycle.
specNote: 90 Hz is an optional Extended Eye Tracking mode; the standard interface is approximately 30 Hz.

name: PCEye
tagline: An eye-tracking peripheral for Windows access
description: PCEye connects over USB and works with TD Control to support eye-based control of a Windows computer.
use: Everyday computer access and assistive communication
review: Evaluate comfort, target selection, and sustained use. Research-data export capabilities require separate confirmation.
specNote: The official support page lists a gaze data rate of 33 Hz.

name: TD Pilot
tagline: iPad-based communication with eye control
description: TD Pilot combines eye access with the iPad platform for users who need assistive communication and device access.
use: iPad access and symbol- or text-based communication
review: Trial the actual communication software, mounting arrangement, and everyday portability. AAC devices and research trackers serve different evaluation goals.
specNote: Check current official system and application compatibility information.

name: TD I-Series
tagline: An integrated Windows eye-control platform
description: TD I-Series combines a display, eye tracking, and communication functions in a dedicated device, with multiple sizes and configurations.
use: Text and symbol communication, and everyday computer access
review: Compare practical accessibility, mounts, speakers, and support. Clearly distinguish generations of I-Series and TD I-Series devices.
specNote: Configurations vary across the series; no single sampling rate is assigned.

name: HIRU
tagline: Eye access for Windows and iPadOS
description: IRISBOND HIRU is a multiplatform eye-access device for compatible Windows and iPadOS environments.
use: Cross-platform assistive access and AAC
review: Check the exact iPad model, OS version, application support, and mounting position. Platform support does not mean every device is plug-and-play.
specNote: Confirm the compatibility list together with the required firmware.

name: Eyegaze Edge
tagline: An eye-controlled communication system
description: Eyegaze Edge combines an eye-tracking camera, tablet, and communication functions, with different camera configurations available.
use: Sustained eye-controlled communication and device access
review: Confirm whether the configuration uses an Encore or Prime camera. Their working distances, monocular/binocular modes, and sampling rates differ and should be trialed separately.
specNote: The website lists Encore at 50 Hz and Prime at 60 Hz; these are not combined into a single device specification.

name: EyeOn series
imageNote: The image shows EyeOn Elite. This is a product-family entry; confirm the specific configuration with the manufacturer.
tagline: EyeTech’s dedicated communication tablets
description: EyeOn is an assistive communication tablet product line presented by EyeTech for communication and access across age groups.
use: AAC, everyday communication, and device access
review: Evaluate the communication tasks and support services. Ask the supplier to specify the eye-tracking hardware, applications, and data-export permissions.
specNote: No uniform sampling rate for the range has been verified from the overview page.

name: Tobii Eye Tracker 5
tagline: Head and eye tracking designed for games
description: Tobii Eye Tracker 5 uses gaze and head movement to enhance interaction in supported PC games.
use: Driving and flight simulation games, and gaze overlays for streaming
review: The official page states that it is incompatible with Pro SDK / Pro Lab and is not licensed to collect eye-tracking research data by default. It is not a direct substitute for a research tracker.
specNote: The page does not disclose research sampling modes suitable for direct comparison. Windows Eye Control is also unsupported.

name: Tobii Pro Nano
tagline: A legacy model replaced by a newer product
description: Tobii’s official discontinued-products directory includes this device and names Tobii Pro Spark as its replacement.
use: Interpreting older papers, reproducing experiments, and planning migrations
review: For existing equipment, use available support documentation to assess maintenance and migration. For a new purchase, compare Tobii Pro Spark and check differences in SDKs, firmware, and data formats.
specNote: Legacy model. This edition does not infer sampling rate from the model name or reuse specifications from its successor.

name: Gazepoint GP3 HD
tagline: Higher-rate recording in the Gazepoint range
description: The GP3 HD 150 Hz model uses USB 3 for behavioral research and UX data collection.
use: UX, market research, and basic experiments
review: Hardware and software can be purchased separately or in bundles. Check the analysis modules, export features, and update period included in the quote.
specNote: This entry covers the 150 Hz model; older materials also describe other versions.

name: aSee Pro
tagline: A screen-based research product from 7invensun
description: 7invensun provides official aSee Pro user guides and safety documentation as part of its eye-movement analysis product range.
use: Research and teaching where Chinese-language support is useful
review: Compare local technical support and compatibility with experimental software. Request version-specific data sheets for sampling rate, accuracy, and SDK licensing.
specNote: The source is the official user-documentation portal; unverified numerical values are left blank.

name: aSee Glasses series
tagline: 7invensun’s wearable eye-tracking family
description: Official materials cover aSee Glasses, while the company’s site presents applications of aSee Glasses Plus.
use: Outdoor behavior, teaching, human factors, and mobile research
review: Chinese-language support and local implementation may be useful. Distinguish Glasses, Plus, and other generations rather than mixing their specifications.
specNote: Check the exact model and firmware; this is a product-family entry.
imageNote: The image shows aSee Glasses Plus. This is a product-family entry; access to the original manufacturer page is restricted.

name: Vida / Vida Go
tagline: An eye-access module for Grid Pad
description: Powered by IntelliGaze 11, Vida is available as a Grid Pad module and through a standalone-camera option.
use: Grid communication and Windows access
review: Trial it in everyday postures and lighting. Clarify regional availability and the mounting configurations of Vida and Vida Go.
specNote: The manufacturer describes 60 Hz operation. Its stated 17 ms recovery time is not the same as end-to-end system latency.

name: Lumin-i
tagline: Smartbox’s eye-access communication solution
description: Lumin-i works with Grid Pad communication devices and is designed for sustained everyday eye access.
use: The Grid ecosystem and assistive communication
review: Prioritize tracking recovery, calibration, and target selection in real use instead of comparing nominal sampling rates alone.
specNote: Confirm the hardware generation and the paired Grid Pad model.

name: ST ONE
tagline: Wearable recording for mobile settings
description: ST ONE provides gaze, pupil, and eye-position data, with streaming and API access.
use: Mobile behavior, slippage studies, and programmable recording
review: Calibration reuse and resistance to slippage are manufacturer design priorities. Test offsets, data loss, and recovery with your participants and activities.
specNote: The official page lists eye tracking at 100 Hz and scene video at 30 FPS.

name: ST ONE Light
tagline: A wearable platform with onboard processing
description: The official ST ONE Light announcement emphasizes onboard image processing and connectivity with Android devices and PCs.
use: Mobile research, wearable interaction, and device integration
review: Onboard processing can reduce dependence on external computing. Confirm its relationship to ST ONE, available data fields, and actual availability before ordering.
specNote: The official announcement lists 100 FPS eye tracking. The image used here illustrates the ST ONE product family.
imageNote: The image illustrates the ST ONE family and should not be used to identify the specific Light hardware version.

name: ST ART
tagline: Eye tracking integrated into optical eyepieces
description: ST ART integrates eye tracking into microscopes and other optical eyepiece devices to provide gaze and eye measurements.
use: Microscopy tasks, optical-device human factors, and gaze interaction
review: A specialized optical integration: check host-device interfaces, eyepiece dimensions, display overlays, and mapping to external video first.
specNote: The official page lists 50 Hz. Installation assumptions for a general-purpose screen tracker do not apply.

name: IntelliGaze / CAM30 series
tagline: The IntelliGaze software and camera ecosystem
description: alea technologies provides IntelliGaze for eye-based communication and Windows access, with several CAM30 hardware generations.
use: Assistive communication, Windows access, and eye-control activities
review: Hardware and software licenses need to match. Check the compatibility of CAM30NT, CAM30NXT, and each software version individually.
specNote: The official support page requires IntelliGaze 11 for CAM30NXT. No single sampling rate is assigned to the entire range.

name: AdHawk MindLink
tagline: A MEMS-based approach to tracking glasses
description: AdHawk MindLink uses MEMS eye sensing without eye-imaging cameras and was introduced as a research-oriented wearable.
use: Comparing wearable methods, low-power sensing, and reproducing existing studies
review: The sensing approach differs from video-based tracking. Evaluate data definitions, synchronization, and task suitability. The current manufacturer site could not be read reliably; availability and support need confirmation.
specNote: The 2021 manufacturer announcement lists 500 samples per second. This launch specification does not establish a currently purchasable configuration.

name: Meta Quest Pro
tagline: An established XR headset with eye and face tracking
description: Meta Quest Pro uses eye and facial signals for avatars and immersive interaction, with related developer interfaces.
use: VR social interaction, gaze interfaces, and reproducing existing studies
review: Check developer licensing, permissions, and SDK device support. This entry is retained as a historical platform; its launch page does not establish current inventory.
specNote: Display refresh rate is not treated as eye-tracking sampling rate. Confirm current availability and support.

name: PlayStation VR2
tagline: Integrated eye tracking in a console VR ecosystem
description: PlayStation VR2 uses eye information in supported PS5 content for gaze-related interaction and rendering.
use: Console VR, immersive experiences, and foveated-rendering examples
review: Sony explicitly states that headset eye tracking is not supported in PC mode. PC connectivity alone does not make it an open research eye tracker.
specNote: PS5 and PC support differ. Raw-data access and developer eligibility require separate verification.
